population.note: FICTIONAL. Cycling arithmetic: ever 25.3% − current 13.1% = 12.2% of adults have used and are off now; ≈8.0 pts of current users are on a second or later course and ≈3.8 pts of the off-now group restarted at least once before stopping again, so (8.0+3.8)/25.3 ≈ 47% cycled. That fits ~35% one-year persistence and restart rates near the top of the 36–47% range: at $39–69 cash, a restart takes a telehealth visit and a pharmacy pickup, so stopping no longer feels permanent. First-course current users ≈5.1 pts: ≈3.8 long persisters from before 2030 plus ≈1.3 pts of genuinely new starters (ever-use rose only 1.3 pts). Of ~273M adults: ≈35.7M current, ≈33.3M used and off now, ≈204M never used. The off-now group is now as large as the on group. Age check: 18–29 6.5% × 52M = 3.4M; 30–49 13.5% × 90M = 12.2M; 50–64 22.5% × 62M = 14.0M; 65+ 8.8% × 69M = 6.1M; total 35.7M ≈ 13.1%. Why current use fell 1.5 pts as prices collapsed: the employer retreat removed weight-only coverage from ≈6M commercial users. About half moved to cash generic; the rest, mostly former tirzepatide and retatrutide users unwilling to step down to semaglutide or unable to fit a monthly cash line into their budget, lapsed. DEXA-advised pauses continue. The middle third fell most (15.0 → 13.5) because it held most of the gated employer plans. The top third fell 18.5 → 15.5 as gated plans ended, partly offset by cash MariTide and retatrutide. The bottom third is flat at 10.3: Medicaid holds, cash generic replaces some imports, and some workers in gated plans lost coverage and dropped out. Imported/counterfeit users fell from ≈3.1M to ≈1.6M. Among ≈2.6M 'calm' subscribers, most are counted here as current users without obesity. Pediatric: ≈0.6% of under-18s (≈440k), mostly adolescents 12+ on generic semaglutide through Medicaid or parental cash. The never-used ≈204M are disproportionately under 30, rural, uninsured, or refusers on principle; refusers are now a smaller and less visible group than in 2030. Many children now live in households where a parent is on, off, or between courses, and generic pens sit in household refrigerators next to the condiments.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the Bridge successor is unchanged at $199/month with a $50 copay, BMI/comorbidity criteria and a counselling visit. ≈1.9M obesity Bridge users × $199 × 12 ≈ $4.5B in 2032, up from $4.3B, because the rate was not renegotiated after generic entry. Part D diabetes fills shifted largely to generic semaglutide under plan formulary rules. Medicare covers ≈18.5% of users ≈ 6.6M (6.1M aged 65+ plus ≈0.5M disabled under-65). Medicaid covers ≈10% ≈ 3.6M users. ≈2.2M are on generic semaglutide at ≈$45 net under existing preferred-drug-list substitution rules (2.2M × $45 × 12 ≈ $1.2B), and ≈1.4M remain on branded agents at the $199 rate (1.4M × $199 × 12 ≈ $3.3B). Gross Medicaid spend is ≈$4.5B, down from ≈$8.4B in 2030. The Indiana and Arkansas waivers are unchanged.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 80+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, with first tirzepatide copies sold domestically. China: generic semaglutide is standard, and Chinese API supplies several US ANDA holders as well as the remaining gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide CAD 40–70. Brazil, Mexico and Turkey have generics. Generic oral semaglutide is sold in most markets outside the US.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Generic collapse for one molecule. Under a Sept 2031 patent settlement, generic injectable semaglutide (equivalents to both Ozempic and Wegovy) entered in Jan 2032, alongside a Novo authorised generic. By mid-2032 eight ANDA holders sell it at $39–69/month cash through Costco, Cost Plus Drugs, Amazon Pharmacy and the federal direct portal. Tirzepatide stays branded (patents to ~2036): Lilly cut the direct price to $179, with no generic. Retatrutide is still $1,499 list and $399 direct. MariTide (monthly, approved May 2031) lists at $1,199 with a $449 direct price. Oral starting doses stay at $149, and US oral semaglutide is still branded. Payer mix of ≈35.7M users: commercial 35% (12.5M; ≈8.0M under T2D/CVD/OSA/CKD codes and ≈4.5M weight-only in remaining plans), Medicare 18.5% (6.6M), Medicaid 10% (3.6M), cash/direct 32% (11.4M, incl. ≈2.6M calm subscribers), imported/counterfeit 4.5% (1.6M) = 100%. This is the two-tier system. Covered branded next-gen care (MariTide, retatrutide, DEXA, coaching) goes mainly to people with qualifying diagnoses or high incomes. Everyone else gets cash generic semaglutide with a $29–49 telehealth script and usually no scan. At $49 the barrier is no longer the price. It is having $49 left over in a given month, a prescriber, and a pharmacy. Wellness surcharges of up to 30% of premium persist in plans that dropped the drug benefit.

GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1/amylin dual agonist, weekly injectable (amycretin, approved Oct 2031)

GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'calm', 'focus' and 'craving freedom' subscriptions, now mostly microdosed generic semaglutide pens at $49–79/month, sold to people without obesity
smoking and vaping cessation (still off-label after the 2029 CRL)
'metabolic health' / longevity regimens in concierge practices, now often using monthly MariTide
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
gambling and compulsive-shopping craving reduction, still anecdotal
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. No new indication this step. The 2032 approvals are all for weight management. MariTide (filed Apr 2030) was approved May 2031 as the first monthly incretin. Its label requires baseline body-composition assessment for users over 50 under the 2029 bone guidance. It is given in clinic or at home, and many covering plans now require clinic administration, which turns adherence from a weekly act into an appointment. Amycretin was approved Oct 2031 after the 72-week DEXA data with a bone-monitoring label, and launch is limited. Survodutide was resubmitted Jun 2031; a decision is pending in early 2033. Bimagrumab combinations are in phase 3 and not on the market. No implant is on the US market; implant programmes are phase 2 or earlier. Novo's new smoking-cessation trial is enrolling and resubmission is not expected before 2033. The incretin market is ≈$104B in 2032, down from ≈$118B: US semaglutide revenue is falling under generic erosion, Lilly growth is slower after the scandal, and MariTide adds ≈$4B annualised. Unit volume is roughly flat. Bone agents remain routine co-prescriptions in covered tiers and are rare in the cash generic tier.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of voluntary stops. Self-titrated generic pens and monthly MariTide dosing produce front-loaded GI episodes in the first days after each dose.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; severe gastroparesis caution retained; generic labels carry the same text.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal confirmation; absolute risk low.
Unchanged magnitudes: lean mass is ~30–40% of loss in untrained users over 50. The concern has moved to the cash generic tier, where body-composition assessment is rare.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 2028 class label and 2029 joint guidance retained; MariTide and amycretin labels include baseline body-composition language.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal. ≈2.8M 65+ users with >2 years' use × ~0.6%/yr baseline × ~0.33 excess ≈ 5,500 excess hip fractures a year against ~300,000 total. The ~1.2× signal in cycling postmenopausal women 50–64 persists. DEXA waits eased to 4–6 weeks as fewer covered plans required scans.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelling and guidance unchanged; FDA keeps bone endpoints in new filings; the DOJ civil case against Novo is still unresolved.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts still conflict; very low absolute risk.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label; FDA warnings mention.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new data beyond the 2030 interim SHAPS findings (~10–14% of top-dose retatrutide users vs ~5% of comparators). The 2031 qui tam complaint alleges Lilly held those interim data for ~9 months before submission. The finding itself is unchanged, but trust in it is not. Calm subscribers (~2.6M) remain unmeasured.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change; FTC warning letters continue; DOJ intervened in the Lilly qui tam (Aug 2031).

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Involuntary stops have shifted from gating failures to coverage terminations under the employer retreat. With cheap restarts, regain-and-restart is now a routine pattern rather than a crisis.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. Indiana waiver litigation still pending in the Seventh Circuit.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signals steady. Under-monitored in cash users.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~7 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of follow-up. Cycling-and-bone concern persists as cycling reaches 47% of ever-users. Interim adolescent bone-accrual results reported no significant deficit at 2 years; the studies are underpowered and continuing.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Poison-centre calls involving imported product fell ~35% from the 2030 peak as $49 domestic generics undercut mail order. Counterfeiters moved to faking branded tirzepatide and retatrutide pens, where the price gap remains. No mass cluster has occurred since Aug 2029.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts and pen-authentication guidance continue; no new law.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated fall-related ED visits in 65+ long-term users persist; confounding still not resolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Bridge counselling template retains fall-risk screening.

food_and_beverage.state: With current use slightly down and normalised, snack volume decline slows to ~1–2% a year. Protein, fibre and 'bone-forward' claims are now table stakes rather than growth lines. Private-label 'GLP-1 friendly' ranges at Kroger and Walmart take share from branded portion packs. The 'real food, full portion' heritage brands plateau as the backlash audience shrinks.

alcohol.state: Fourth and fifth years of US spirits volume decline, but at a slower rate. Calm subscriptions keep eroding the unwinding occasion among 25–44 professionals. Beer is flat and non-alcoholic lines are growing. Tobacco and vape quit rates stay elevated.

restaurants.state: Half portions and on/off menus are now invisible defaults. Traffic is flat and check sizes are stable. The Atlanta and Memphis 'no-gram' rooms remain local institutions but are no longer a national story. Buffet closures have slowed because the remaining units serve the off-drug and never-users.

apparel.state: Size churn continues because nearly half of ever-users cycle. Resale and rental of 'between-course' wardrobes grows. Plus-size specialists hold steady, serving never-users and the off-now population of ≈33M.

fitness.state: Prescribed lifting and DEXA-plus-coaching chains stop growing as employer and some MA conditions fall away, and they now serve mainly the covered tier. Mobile DEXA vans are idle more often. Budget gyms market 'generic plus barbell' packages to cash users.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage falls from 63% to 44%. Most plans now cover incretins only under T2D, cardiovascular, OSA and CKD codes, with generic semaglutide as step one, and members are pointed to $49 cash. PBMs suspended outcome-guarantee contracts after the Lilly scandal. Pharmacy trend falls to ~+3%. Bone and fracture costs remain in models for covered users.

pharma.state: Novo loses US semaglutide revenue to generics and an authorised generic it sells itself. Lilly still leads volume through tirzepatide and retatrutide but faces DOJ intervention in the qui tam, a ~20% share-price drawdown and suspended PBM outcome contracts. Amgen's MariTide wins the covered and concierge tiers. Generic makers (Teva, Viatris, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's, Hikma and others) run a low-margin volume business.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it no longer signals anything. It is like wearing glasses. Being off is what draws a question, and people answer with a short script: 'my DEXA', 'between courses', 'my plan dropped it'. Visible regain is read as a budget event, not a moral one. Resistance-trained shoulders still mark the covered tier, and the forward-stooped 'too long on it' look in people over 60 is now unremarked rather than discussed.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The gradient is in what people are on and how they are monitored, not in whether they are on. The top third runs monthly MariTide or retatrutide with scans and antiresorptives. The middle third, many dropped by employers in January 2032, buys generic semaglutide at Costco with no scan. The bottom third is on Medicaid generics, cash generics when the month allows, or imports. In suburban Columbus, Ohio, office workers compare pharmacies, not drugs.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Smaller protein-first plates are simply how people eat. Hosts no longer plan three menus, because guests eat whatever amount they want and nobody remarks on it. Church potlucks in the Tulsa–Dallas corridor still frame full plates as fellowship, but with fewer people making the point.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Hinge and Bumble removed the on/off profile field in 2032 because most profiles listed 'on' and it stopped sorting anyone. 'Unmedicated' survives as a filter only on small niche apps. Calm-subscription mismatches are still a staple of advice columns.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a setting people adjust. The 2030 backlash coalition has thinned. The Atlanta body-sovereignty collectives remain active locally and refocus on fat people's access to unrelated medical care. The religious 'appetite is a gift' strand persists in its congregations. Supplement influencers lost their price argument to $49 generics. Normalisation also produced a quieter stigma: the never-users, about three-quarters of adults, are disproportionately the poor, the rural and the uninsured, and in professional settings they are asked to explain themselves.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. No new systematic data. The 2030 interim SHAPS figures (~10–14% of top-dose retatrutide users crossing a clinical threshold vs ~5% of comparators) remain the only near-trial-grade evidence. The Lilly qui tam made them famous without changing them. Calm subscribers have grown from ~1.5–2M to ≈2.6M, nearly all on microdosed generic semaglutide, and none are systematically measured.
interior_life.framing: Sold as a feature and priced as a commodity. 'Quiet' cut its price from $149 to $59 on generic microdose pens, and 'Even' and 'Unhooked' followed. The copy is unchanged: calm, focus, less noise. Clinicians say 'reward modulation', users say 'the grey', and the FTC keeps writing letters. After the scandal, 'the grey' also carries suspicion: people ask whether the company knew.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Employers that dropped weight coverage often still reimburse calm subscriptions through lifestyle-spending accounts, which are cheaper than a benefit and carry no gating. So the company now pays for the mood effect but not for the weight effect. Fleets still favour drivers staying on for DOT sleep-apnea reasons. Sales and hospitality workers still skip doses before big days. MariTide users describe the monthly shot as 'set and forget', and some note a flatter week after each dose.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Written unmedicated' is now a niche marketing claim in Nashville rather than a movement. Discourse about 'grey albums' persists. Extreme-stimulus leisure (spicy food, loud venues, adventure travel) stays elevated among subscribers and is no longer remarked on.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Dose-holiday weekends are harder on monthly MariTide, and couples on it talk about 'week three', when the effect fades. Sex therapists still screen for dose. Calm couples report fewer fights and less desire.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Mostly about price and coverage. The Lilly scandal and the gap between Medicare's $199 rate and $49 generics are stump material for both parties, but no bill has passed. Disability advocates keep pressing the Indiana and Arkansas waiver suits. Consultants still test 'calm voter' messaging and still do not publish it.

state.regulatory_posture: No new state action. The FDA approves generic ANDAs, MariTide and amycretin through ordinary review and keeps bone data requirements. Enforcement is continuation: import alerts, seizures, FTC advertising letters, and DOJ intervention in a private qui tam. Congress held hearings on the Lilly documents and on the Medicare $199 rate but passed no law.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. The Medicare Bridge successor is unchanged at $199/month with a $50 copay. Some beneficiaries now pay more in copay than the $49 generic cash price, and some pay cash instead. Medicaid stays state by state under existing preferred-drug-list rules.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Indiana and Arkansas waivers are unchanged. Private gating shrank with the employer retreat, and plans that still cover now verify adherence through clinic-administered monthly injections rather than days-covered algorithms. Weigh-in kiosks remain in pharmacy chains but see less traffic. BMI-linked wellness surcharges of up to 30% persist, including in plans that no longer cover the drug.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT sleep-apnea screening still makes tirzepatide or generic semaglutide a de facto requirement for some drivers. Army accession policy is unchanged and contested. Fleet DEXA screening for drivers over 55 continues.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Chinese and Indian API now supply legitimate US generics as well as the gray trade, which makes the 2030 'seal the mail' rhetoric awkward. Section 232 tariffs remain, and generic makers absorb them on thin margins. India–US talks drop mail-order pharma as a bargaining chip as import volume falls.

events.event: A whistleblower complaint unsealed in federal court alleges Eli Lilly held interim retatrutide anhedonia data for about nine months before submitting it to the FDA and paid speaker fees to clinicians staffing 'calm' telehealth brands that prescribed low-dose Foundayo; Lilly shares fall 18% in a week and the Justice Department intervenes in August

FDA approves Amgen's MariTide, the first once-monthly weight-loss injection, with baseline body-composition monitoring in the label; it launches in July at $1,199 list and $449 direct, and covering plans begin requiring clinic administration

Novo Nordisk settles patent litigation with generic filers, clearing entry for generic injectable semaglutide in January 2032; by June eight makers and a Novo authorised generic sell it at $39–69 a month cash at Costco, Cost Plus and Amazon

With PBM outcome-guarantee contracts suspended after the Lilly allegations, a benefits-consultancy survey finds the share of employers covering weight management has fallen from 63% to 44%; most plans now cover incretins only under diabetes, cardiac, sleep-apnea and kidney codes, with generic semaglutide first

'Quiet' cuts its calm subscription from $149 to $59 by switching to microdosed generic semaglutide pens; rivals follow, subscribers across brands pass an estimated 2.6 million, and the FTC sends a fresh round of warning letters
Hinge and Bumble remove the 'on/off GLP-1' profile field, saying more than 70% of users who filled it in chose 'on' and the field no longer helped anyone match

open_tensions: Medicare still pays $199 a month for branded incretins with a $50 copay while generic semaglutide sells for $39–69 cash. That is about $4.5B a year in Bridge spending that nobody has renegotiated, and some beneficiaries now pay cash to avoid their own copay.

The two tiers have hardened. Monitored branded care (MariTide, retatrutide, DEXA, bone agents) goes to the diagnosed and the well-off, and unmonitored cash generic goes to everyone else. The bone and lean-mass guidance now applies mostly to the people least likely to receive it.

Employers that dropped weight coverage still fund calm subscriptions through lifestyle accounts, paying for the mood effect while refusing the medical one. The only trial-grade anhedonia data now sit inside a DOJ case against the dominant manufacturer.

Off-drug is now as large a population as on-drug (≈33M vs ≈36M adults), and 47% of ever-users cycle. The cycling-and-bone signal in postmenopausal women is unresolved, while cheap restarts make cycling the default way people use the drug.
still_true: The Indiana and Arkansas Medicaid 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins; two misses end coverage for 12 months, and the disability-rights litigation is still pending in the Seventh Circuit.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.
The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge successor still pays $199/month with the $50 beneficiary copay, BMI/comorbidity criteria and the counselling-visit requirement.
Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
Wellness rules still allow BMI-linked premium surcharges of up to 30% of premium.

prose.headline: $49 at Costco, No Coverage Required: The Weight Drug Is Finally Cheap, and Fewer Americans Are Taking It
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 about one American adult in eight is on an incretin drug, slightly fewer than two years ago, even though the drug that started it now costs less than a phone bill. In January generic semaglutide reached American pharmacies under a patent settlement Novo Nordisk signed the previous autumn. By summer eight manufacturers and Novo's own authorised generic were selling it for $39 to $69 a month at Costco, Cost Plus and Amazon. For most of the decade the question had been whether you could afford it. Now the question is whether you have forty-nine dollars left in a given month, a prescriber who will write the script, and nobody checking your bones.

Employers read the generic price as permission to stop paying. Their earlier deal, with pharmacy-benefit managers offering low net prices in exchange for verified weigh-ins and a five-percent response threshold, broke down in 2031. A whistleblower complaint alleged that Eli Lilly had held interim data on retatrutide's pleasure-dampening effect for nine months and had paid clinicians who staffed 'calm' telehealth brands. The PBMs suspended their outcome guarantees, and the Justice Department joined the case. Employer coverage for weight management fell from about two-thirds of firms to under half. Most plans now pay only when there is a diabetes, heart, sleep-apnea or kidney code, and they start with the generic. Everyone else is told about the Costco price.

Some of those people made the switch and many did not. Former tirzepatide users did not want to go back to a weaker molecule at their own expense, and a monthly line item is a real cost in a household that is already stretched. The number of Americans who have used these drugs and are off them now roughly equals the number on them. Almost half of everyone who has ever started has stopped and restarted at least once. Restarting takes a $29 video visit.

The covered tier looks different. In May 2031 Amgen's MariTide became the first once-a-month injection, and plans that still cover weight loss like it because the shot is given in a clinic and can be verified. For people on it, adherence is an appointment rather than a decision made every Sunday night. They also get a DEXA scan, a strength coach and, if needed, an infusion of zoledronic acid. The cash tier gets a pen and a printout. The bone data have not changed: about five and a half thousand extra hip fractures a year among older long-term users, and a smaller excess in women in their fifties who cycle. The guidance is now aimed mostly at people who never see a scanner.

Medicare has not changed either. It still pays $199 a month with a $50 copay, a rate agreed before the generics arrived. Some retirees now pay cash rather than their own copay. Congress held a hearing on this and passed nothing.

The quieting effect keeps selling. 'Quiet' cut its subscription from $149 to $59 by switching to microdosed generic pens, and its rivals followed. About 2.6 million Americans, most of whom were never heavy, now buy calm by mail, often through the same employer lifestyle accounts whose companies stopped covering the drug for obesity. Users still call the effect 'the grey'. Since the Lilly complaint, they also ask who knew about it.

In August the big dating apps dropped the on/off profile field because almost everyone who filled it in said 'on'. In suburban Columbus office workers compare pharmacies, not doses. Being on the drug no longer means anything. Being off requires a short explanation: my scan, my plan, between courses. Snack volumes slip a little and spirits keep falling. From the outside things look settled.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Ochoa wakes at 5:40 in Mesa and checks the butter shelf of the refrigerator. One generic pen is left, CostcoRx, $49. She bought her first box in February, after the dental group's new plan dropped Zepbound unless you had a diabetes code, and she doesn't. Sunday is her injection day, and today is Thursday.

At the office the hygienists eat salads from the same place. Marisol eats a full burrito. Somebody asks, kindly, whether she came off. "My DEXA," Marisol says, and that ends it.

At lunch Denise renews her script on her phone. A nurse practitioner in another state asks four questions in nine minutes. Denise asks whether she should get a bone scan, since she's fifty-three. The NP says it's recommended and that her primary care office can order one. Denise doesn't have a primary care office anymore. She writes DEXA on a sticky note and puts it on the dashboard, next to an older note that says DEXA.

After work she picks up Ray's Wegovy at Walgreens. He's sixty-seven, it goes through Medicare, and his copay is fifty dollars. Hers is forty-nine. Every time they say this out loud, they laugh.

Their daughter Bree calls from Austin. Her company pays for 'Quiet' out of the lifestyle account. She says she's fine, really, just tired of everything being loud. Denise hears the TV on mute behind her.

In bed Denise works out August. There's the car registration and Ray's crown, which insurance only half covers. She could skip a month. People do. You start again, and nobody asks.

least_plausible_claims.quote: saying more than 70% of users who filled it in chose 'on' and the field no longer helped anyone match
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: only 6.5% of 18–29s and 13.5% of 30–49s are on the drug, so a 70%+ 'on' share among dating-app users sits badly with the world's own prevalence figures. Self-selection is not shown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Being on it no longer signals anything. It is like wearing glasses. Being off is what draws a question
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude and mechanism: 13.1% of adults are on and about three-quarters have never used, so being off is the overwhelming norm. The same world says never-users are 'asked to explain themselves', and the glasses analogy fits only a small professional subset.

least_plausible_claims.quote: With PBM outcome-guarantee contracts suspended after the Lilly allegations
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: allegations about delayed retatrutide anhedonia data are asserted to make PBMs suspend outcome contracts for all GLP-1s and employers drop coverage. No chain is shown from one manufacturer's reporting delay to suspending contracts on semaglutide and tirzepatide.

rationale.badness: Cheap generics widen access and ease gating, so autonomy and cohesion improve on 2030. But the two-tier split (monitored MariTide/DEXA care for the diagnosed and wealthy, unmonitored $49 pens for everyone else) leaves the bone and lean-mass guidance aimed at the people least likely to get scanned. Roughly 2.6M unmeasured 'calm' users, employer-funded mood subscriptions, a 47% cycling rate and a Lilly data scandal that undermines trust in the anhedonia evidence keep this at a harder but not dystopian world.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: every driver is visible: adoption −1.5pp (14.6→13.1), generic_collapse via the Sept 2031 settlement event, employer retreat 63→44%, no new indications, no new safety signal, MariTide approved 13 months after filing, the Lilly scandal, normalisation, no state action, and the marketed calm layer. mechanism: the generic→cash and employer-retreat chain is mostly shown, including the ≈6M commercial users and the half-moved/half-lapsed split. But the PBM suspension after one Lilly dataset is asserted (claim 3), and the 'like wearing glasses' normalisation (claim 2) overreaches. magnitude: figures sit inside the envelope (ever-use 25.3, current 13.1, income thirds average to 13.1, age bands sum to 35.7M). Payer mix, Bridge $4.5B, Medicaid $4.5B and 5,500 hip fractures all reconcile. Small gaps are 'unit volume roughly flat' against about 9% fewer users, and the dating-app 70% figure (claim 1).
rationale.generativity: The prose has a concrete, filmable cast: Denise in Mesa with the pen in the butter shelf, Marisol's 'My DEXA', Ray's $50 Medicare copay against her $49 cash price, and Bree's muted TV and 'Quiet' subscription. Details such as the sticky note repeating DEXA and the generic pens beside the condiments imply scenes. Small flaws: the 'end of 2032' framing sits oddly with Denise budgeting for 'August', and some world fields explain more than they show.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Being on it no longer signals anything. It is like wearing glasses.
